la:verb:caelo.html:
caelo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
1. caelum
.
Lit., answering to the Gr. τορεύω, to engrave in relief upon metals (esp. silver) or wory, to make raised work, to carve, engrave; later also, to cast (cf. O. Müll. Archaeol. § 311 sq.; and v. , s. v. caelatura; Fest. s. v. ancaesa, p. 17; ; ; )' ab initio sic opus ducere, ut caelandum, non ex integro fabricandum sit, : hanc speciem Praxiteles caelavit argento,: galeas aere Corinthio,: caelata in auro Fortia facta patrum,: clipeo quoque flumina septem Argento partim, partim caelaverat auro,; cf. ; 13, 684: scuta auro, argento, Liv 9, 40, 2; 7, 10, 7: vasa magnifica et pretiose caelata,: vasa caelata,; ; ; centauros in scyphis,: libidines in poculis, id. prooem. § 4 al.; Liv 23, 24, 12: caelatum aurum et argentum,; ; ; ; : caelata metus alios arma,: Phorcys caelatus Gorgone parmam,.—
To carve or engrave on other materials (cf. caelatura, I. B.); upon wood: pocula ponam Fagina, caelatum divini opus Alcimedontis,; in marble: caelavit Scopas pteron ab oriente,; cf.: (vitrum) argenti modo caelatur,; .—
Meton. of other works of art.
Of skilful weaving or embroidering: velamina caelata multā arte,.—
Of poetry: carmina compono, hio elegos. Mirabile visu Caelatumque novem musis (i. e. a novem musis) opus, * .—
Trop.: quem modo caelatum stellis Delphina videbas, i. e. the constellation,.

la:other:Caesar.html:
Caesar, ăris (CAESERIS, C. I. L. 4, 2308; : CAESARVS, C. I. L. 1, 696), m., = Καῖσαρ [a caeso matris utero, ; cf. :
a caesarie dictus, qui scilicet cum caesarie natus est,; cf. Comment. p. 383. Both etymm. also in , and . Better acc. to Doed. Syn. III. p. 17, from caesius, caeruleus, the color of the skin; cf. Rufus], a cognomen in the gens Julia. Of these the most celebrated, C.Julius Caesar, distinguished as general, orator, statesman, and author, was assassinated by Brutus and Cassius, B.C. 44. After him all the emperors bore the name Caesar, with the title Augustus, until, under Adrian, this difference arose: Augustus designated the ruling emperor; Caesar, the heir to the throne, the crown-prince, etc., ; .—

Caesărīnus, a, um, adj., of or relating to the triumvir Julius Cœsar, Cœsarian: celeritas, Orell. N.cr.—
Caesărĭānus, a, um, adj.
Of the triumvir Cœsar, Cœsarian: bellum civile,.— Hence, Caesărĭāni, ōrum, m., the adherents of Cœsar in the civil war (as Pompeiani, his opponents), : orationes, orations of Cicero in which Cœsar was praised (pro Marcello, Deiotaro, De Provinciis Consularibus, etc.), .—
Imperial, Vop. Carin. init.: Pallas (esp. honored by Domitian),.—Hence, subst.
Caesărĭāni, ōrum, m.
A class of provincial imperial officers, ; ; Cod. Th. 10, 7.—
Partisans of Cœsar, Auct. B. Afr. 13; .—
Caesărĭānum, i, n., a kind of eye-salve, , n. 27.—
Caesă-rĕus, a, um, adj.
Of or pertaining to the triumvir Cœsar, Cœsarian (mostly poet.): sanguis,: Penates,: Vesta,: forum,founded by him,.—
Imperial: amphitheatrum,built by the emperor Domitian,: leones,presented by Domitian in the fight of wild beasts,.

la:adj:caecus.html:
caecus (not coecus; sometimes in MSS. cēcus), a, um, adj.
akin to σκιά, σκότος; Sanscr. khāyā, shadow
,
having no light, devoid of light.
Act., not seeing, blind.
Lit.: Appius, qui caecus annos multos fuit,: traditum est enim Homerum caecum fuisse,; : catuli, qui jam dispecturi sunt, caeci aeque et hi qui modo nati,: si facie miserabili senis, caeci, infantis,: caecum corpus,the blind part of the body, the back,: perdices caecae impetu,: gigni,.—
Prov.: ut si Caecus iter monstrare velit,: apparet id quidem etiam caeco,even a blind man can see that,: caecis hoc, ut aiunt, satis clarum est,.—
Trop., mentally or morally blind, blinded (freq. in prose and poetry): o pectora caeca!: non solum ipsa Fortuna caeca est, sed eos etiam plerumque efficit caecos, quos complexa est,; cf. casus,: caecus atque amens tribunus,: caecum me et praecipitem ferri,: mater caeca crudelitate et scelere,: cupidine,: amentiā,: quem mala stultitia Caecum agit,: amatorem amicae Turpia decipiunt caecum vitia,: mens,.—With ad: caecus ad has belli artes,.—With gen.: caecus animi,; : fati futuri,ignorant of,; cf. .—Subst.: Caeci, ōrum, m., the blind people, i.e. the people of Chalcedon, according to the oracle at Delphi. ; cf. . —
Meton. of the passions themselves: caeca honorum cupido,; : ac temeraria dominatrix animi cupiditas,; : exspectatio,: amor,: amor sui,: festinatio,: furor,: caeca et sopita socordia,: ambitio,.—
Pregn., blind, i.e. at random, vague, indiscriminate, aimless: in hac calumniā timoris et caecae suspitionis tormento,: caeco quodam timore... quaerebant aliquem ducem,: caecique in nubibus ignes Terrificant animos,: caeca regens filo vestigia,: ne sint caecae, pater, exsecrationes tuae,: et caeco flentque paventque metu,: lymphatis caeco pavore animis,: cervus... Caeco timore proximam villam petit,: timor,.—
Transf.
Of plants, without buds or eyes: rami,; cf. caeco and oculus. —
Of the large intestine: intestinum,the cœcum,; .—
Pass., that cannot be seen, or trop., that cannot be known, invisible, concealed, hidden, secret, obscure, dark.
Lit.: sunt igitur venti nimirum corpora caeca, winds are accordingly bodies, although invisible, ; ; ; 2, 713: vallum caecum,; cf.: caecum vallum dicitur, in quo praeacuti pali terrae affixi herbis vel frondibus occuluntur, Paul. ex Müll.; so, fossae,covered,; . 1: in vada caeca ferre,: fores,private,: spiramenta,: colubri,: ignis,: venenum,: tabes,: viae,blind ways,: insidiae armaque,; cf. : saxa,; : vulnus,a secret wound,; but also,a wound upon the back,; cf. in the same sense, ictus,; (cf.: caecum corpus, the back, I. A. supra): caeca manus, i.e. abscondita,: caecum domūs scelus,.—
Trop.: caecas exponere causas,: improba navigii ratio, tum caeca jacebat,lay still concealed,; so, venti potestas,; : fluctus, Sisenn. ap. : caeca et clandestina natura,: res caecae et ab aspectūs judicio remotae,: obscurum atque caecum,: fata,: sors,: tumultus,secret conspiracies,: amor,; cf.: stimulos in pectore caecos Condidit,. In Plaut. once, prob. taken from the vulgar lang.: caecā die emere, upon a concealed (pay-) day, i.e. to purchase on credit (opp. oculata dies, i.e. for ready money): Ca. Pereo inopiā argentariā. Ba. Emito die caecā hercle olivom, id vendito oculatā die, .—
By poet. license, transf. to the hearing: murmur, (as we, by a similar meton., say a hollow sound; cf. on the other hand, in Gr. τυφλὸς τὰ ὦτα); so, clamor,: mugitusterrae,.—
Neutr., that obstructs the sight, or trop., the perception; dark, gloomy, thick, dense, obscure.
Lit.: nox,; ; ; ; : caligo,; ; ; ; : tenebrae,; ; ; 3, 87; 6, 35; 3, 87: silentia, i.e. nox,: latebrae,: iter,: loca,: cavernae,; : latus,: cubiculum si fenestram non habet, dicitur caecum, Müll.; so, domus,without windows,: parietes,: pulvis,: carcer,: sardonyches,not transparent, opaque,: smaragdi,: acervus (of chaos), chaotic, confused, Ov M. 1, 24; ' chaos, , .—
Trop., uncertain, doubtful: obscurā spe et caecā exspectatione pendere, i.e. of an uncertain consequence or result, : quod temere fit caeco casu,. cursus (Fortunae), : eventus,: caeci morbi, quorum causas ne medici quidem perspicere queunt,; so, dolores,; : crimen,that cannot be proved,.— Subst.: caecum, i, n., uncertainty, obscurity (poet.): verum in caeco esse,.—* Comp., .—Sup. and adv. not in. use.

la:verb:caedo.html:
caedo, cĕcīdi (in MSS. freq. caecīdi, v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 460), caesum, 3, v. a.
root cīd- for scid-; cf. scindo; Gr. σχίζω
.
Lit.
In gen.
To cut, hew, lop, cut down, fell, cut off, cut to pieces: caesa abiegna trabes, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 281 Vahl.): frondem querneam caedito,: arbores,; : robur,; : lignum,. 63: silvam, Varr ap. ; ; ; ; ; : nemus,; cf. ; 9, 230; 9, 374; 14, 535: harundinem,: arboris auctum,: comam vitis,: faenum,: murus latius quam caederetur ruebat,: caesis montis fodisse medullis,; so, caedi montis in marmora,, prooem. § 2: lapis caedendus,: silicem,: marmor,: toga rotunda et apte caesa,cut out,: caedunt securibus umida vina, with axes they cut out the wine (formerly liquid, now frozen), : volutas, to carve or hollow out volutes, : tineae omnia caedunt, Lucil. ap. .—
Prov.: ut vineta egomet caedam mea,i. e. carry my own hide to market, (proverbium in eos dicitur, qui sibi volentes nocent, Schol. Crucq.; cf. ; ).—
Ruta caesa; v ruo, P. a.—
In gen., to strike upon something, to knock at, to beat, strike, cudgel, etc.: ut lapidem ferro quom caedimus evolat ignis,strike upon with iron,: caedere januam saxis,: silicem rostro,: vasa dolabris,: femur, pectus, frontem,; cf. : verberibus,; so : pugnis,,

43: aliquem ex occulto,: at validis socios caedebant dentibus apri,they fell with their strong tusks upon their own party,; cf. : virgis ad necem caedi,; : populum saxis,: ferulā aliquem,: flagris,: aliquem loris,; ; ; : caeduntur (agrestes) inter potentium inimicitias, Dietsch: nudatos virgis,: hastilibus caedentes terga trepidantium,: servum sub furcā caesum medio egerat circo, i.e. ita ut simul caederet,.—

Prov.: stimulos pugnis caedere,to kick against the pricks, to aggravate a danger by foolish resistance,.—
Trop.: in judicio testibus caeditur,is pressed, hard pushed,.—
Pregn.
(Cf. cado, I. B. 2.) To strike mortally, to kill, murder: ille dies, quo Ti. Gracchus est caesus,: P. Africanus de Tiberio Graccho responderat jure caesum videri,; : caeso Argo,; ; ; 12, 590; 12, 603; —Poet., transf. to the blood shed in slaying: caeso sparsuros sanguine flammam,.—Esp. freq.,
In milit. lang., to slay a single enemy; or, when a hostile army as a whole is spoken of, to conquer with great slaughter, to cut to pieces, vanquish, destroy (cf. Oud., Wolf, and Baumg.Crus. upon ): exercitus caesus fususque,: Romani insecuti (hostem), caedentes spoliantesque caesos, castra regia diripiunt,; : infra arcem caesi captique multi mortales,; and 9; ; ; ; : Indos,: passim obvios,: praesidium,: propugnatores reipublicae,: caesus (hostis) per calles saltusque vagando circumagatur, Kreyss.: consulem exercitumque caesum,: legio-nes nostras cecidere,; so ; ; .— And poet., the leader is put for the army: Pyrrhum et ingentem cecidit Antiochum Hannibalemque dirum,.—In poet. hypallage: caesi corporum acervi (for caesorum),.—
To slaughter animals, esp. for offerings, to kill, slay, sacrifice: caedit greges armentorum,: boves,: deorum mentes caesis hostiis placare,: caesis victimis,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; Ov.M.13, 637; ; ; ; 12, 3 al.: inter caesa et porrecta; v. porricio.—
Hence, since security for a person was anciently given by the deposit of sheep belonging to him, which were slaughtered in case of forfeiture, leg. t. t.: pignus caedere (or concidere), to declare the for feiture of a security, to confiscate a pledge: non tibi illa sunt caedenda, si L. Crassum vis coërcere, Crass. ap. .—
In mal. part. ( = concido; cf.: jam hoc, caede, concide: nonne vobis verba depromere videtur ad omne genus nequitiae accommodata?); ; ; .—
Trop.: caedere sermones, a Grecism, acc. to P., = κόπτειν τὰ ῥήματα, to chop words, chat, talk, converse, ; cf. , and P.: oratio caesa,i. e. asyndeton,; Aquil. Rom. §§ 18 and 19; ; .—Hence, caesum, i, n.; subst. in gram. synon. with comma, a stop, pause, comma, ; Aquil. Rom. § 19; .

Caelĭus (Coel-), i, m.
A Roman gentile name.
The orator M. Caelius Rufus, for whom Cicero made an oration, and whose letters to Cicero are contained in the 8th book of the Epp. ad Famil.; ; sqq.; ; ; ; v. Teuffel, Röm. Litt. § 206, 5 sqq.—Hence, Caelĭānus, a, um, adj., Cœlian: orationes,.—
L. Caelius Antipater, a distinguished historian and jurist in the time of the Gracchi, and teacher of Crassus, ; ; .—Hence, Caelĭāna, ōrum, n., the writings of Cœlius, ; v. Teuffel. Röm. Litt. § 142.—
C. Caelius Caldus, an orator, contemporary with Crassus, ; ; .—
Caelius Aurelianus, a physician of the post - classic period, v. Teuffel, Röm. Litt. § 456.—
Caelius Mons, the Cœlian Hill at Rome, south of Palatinus, and east of Aventinus, named after the Tuscan Caeles Vibenna (pure Etrusc. Kaile Fipne), now the Lateran Mount, Varr L. L. 5, § 46 Müll.; ; ; .—Called Caelius Major, ; cf. Caeliolus.—The soldiers of this Caeles are calledCaelĭāni, Müll.; cf.: CAELIANVS EXERCITVS,.

senses: the act of cutting or lopping something off

la:noun:caedes.html:
caedes, is (
gen. plur. regularly caedium, ; ; ; but caedum,; ; ; 4, 796; 5, 220; 10, 233; ; ; cf. P), f.
caedo
.
Lit.
In gen., a cutting or lopping off (post-class. and rare): ligni atque frondium caedes,: capilli, qui caede cultrorum desecti,.—
Esp. (acc. to caedo, I. B. 1.; cf. cado, I. B. 2.), a cutting down, slaughter, massacre, carnage; esp. in battle or by an assassin; murder (usu. class. signif. of the word in prose and poetry; esp. freq. in the histt. in Suet. alone more than twenty times): pugnam caedesque petessit,: caedem caede accumulantes,: caedem (the deadly slaughter, conflict) in quā P. Clodius occisus est, : caedes et occisio,: magistratuum privatorumque caedes,: cum in silvā Silā facta caedes esset,: notat (Catilina) et designat oculis ad caedem unumquemque nostrum,: jam non pugna sed caedes erat,: caedes inde, non jam pugna fuit,: ex mediā caede effugere,: cum caedibus et incendiis agrum perpopulari,: silvestres homines... Caedibus et victu foedo deterruit Orpheus,: magnā caede factā multisque occisis,: caedes civium,: caedem in aliquem facere,; : edere,; ; : perpetrare,: committere,; ; ; ; : admittere,: peragere,: abnuere,: festinare,: ab omni caede abhorrere,: portendere, Sall.J. 3, 2; et saep.; cf. in the poets,; ; ; ; ; ; 3, 24, 26; 4, 4, 59; ; ; ; 4, 160; 5, 69; 6, 669.—
The slaughter of animals, esp. of victims: studiosus caedis ferinae, i. e. ferarum,; so ; cf. ferarum,; 15, 106: armenti,: boum,: juvenci,: bidentium,: juvencorum,.—
Meton.
(Abstr. pro concreto.) The persons slain or murdered, the slain: caedis acervi,: plenae caedibus viae,.—
Also meton. as in Gr. φόνος, the blood shed by murder, gore, ; : permixta flumina caede,: respersus fraternā caede,: madefient caede sepulcra,: tepidā recens Caede locus,: sparsae caede comae,: caede madentes,; ; ; 4, 97; 4, 125; 4, 163; 6, 657; 8, 444; 9, 73; 13, 389; 15, 174.—
An attempt to murder: nostrae injuria caedis,.—
A striking with the fist, a beating (post-class.): contumeliosa, Don. : nimia,; 2, 1, 18.
